lesson_title: The Paving Slab That Built the Karoo
hook_text: Drop a concrete slab on a sand heap, add rain, and you've built every flat-topped hill in South Africa.
clip_script: Do this experiment in your head. A builder leaves a heap of soft building sand in a yard, and drops one concrete paving slab flat on top of it. Then the rainy season arrives. Everywhere the rain hits bare sand, it strips it away. But directly under the slab the sand cannot be touched. Weeks later the yard is nearly level — except for one proud column of sand wearing its slab like a flat roof. That yard is the Karoo. The sand is soft shale. The slab is dolerite, ancient molten rock set hard as concrete between the layers. Soft goes first, hard survives — differential erosion, the only rule this landscape obeys. Now watch the shapes. The unbroken high ground is the plateau. Cut a chunk off, still wider than it is tall: a mesa, the box. Trim it until it stands taller than it is wide: a butte, the tower — near Steynsburg two of them pose together as Teebus and Koffiebus, the tea tin and the coffee tin. Then the slab finally fails, and the hill rounds into a tent: the conical hill, like Spandau Kop outside Graaff-Reinet. Strangest of all, the cliffs never grow old — they walk backwards across the country at full steepness, sweeping out the great Karoo plain behind them. Floor, box, tower, tent, flat. One slab, five shapes, a hundred million years.
visual_style: A paving slab on a sand heap in time-lapse rain morphing into a Karoo panorama, hills snapping through box, tower and tent silhouettes with each name stamped on screen, a cliff striding backwards leaving a swept plain.
mood: Backyard-experiment curiosity opening out into deep-time awe.
pacing: Fast build on the sand-heap experiment, rhythmic beats through the five shapes, slow reveal on the walking wall.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read a hundred million years off the next flat-topped koppie you pass.
